cases.query: When can I strip vertical concrete formwork after a pour?

answers.auricrux-fca:
Auricrux construction corpus response (grounded, no live model reachable):

1. CSI Division 03 Concrete — Concrete placement, curing, and formwork sequencing for commercial work. Verify mix design, cold-weather protections, and strength tests before stripping forms. Break cylinders at 7 and 28 days; do not strip vertical forms before initial set or slabs before 500-750 psi per ACI 347 guidance.

2. Concrete Pumping and Placement Logistics — Line pump vs. boom pump selection depends on pour volume, access, and vertical reach. Pre-pour checklist: verify pump pad stability, prime lines with grout slug, maintain slump within spec at discharge, and never add water at the chute without engineer approval. Coordinate truck spacing (one every 20–30 minutes for large slabs) to avoid cold joints.

3. CSI Division 09 Painting and Coatings — Sequence painting after drywall finishing, HVAC balancing dust settles, and prior to flooring installation. Verify moisture content of substrates and manufacturer-required recoat windows; document VOC compliance for occupied buildings.

Apply these to your specific scope, verify against project documents/local AHJ requirements, and confirm with your competent person or PE of record before field execution.
answers.cursor-agent: Vertical formwork (walls/columns) is stripped when the concrete has enough strength to carry its own weight plus construction loads â€” not on a fixed clock alone. Follow the project specs / ACI 347 / engineer of record: many specs allow vertical form removal after concrete reaches a stated psi (often around early strength from field-cured cylinders) or after a minimum time at a given temperature. Do not strip based on calendar hours if it was cold or the mix was slow. Before stripping: confirm no honeycombing that needs repair access first, shore if the member is still load-critical, and never strip slabs/soffits on the same criteria as vertical forms (horizontal needs higher strength, often ~70% of f'c or as specified). cases.query: At what height does OSHA require fall protection in construction?

answers.auricrux-fca:
Auricrux construction corpus response (grounded, no live model reachable):

1. OSHA Fall Protection — Fall protection triggers at 6 ft in construction (29 CFR 1926.501). Inspect harnesses and anchor points daily; guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest systems are the three accepted control methods. A competent person must evaluate the work area continuously.

2. Silica Dust and Respiratory Protection — OSHA's respirable crystalline silica standard (1926.1153) requires engineering controls (wet cutting, vacuum dust collection) for concrete cutting/grinding tasks, with a written exposure control plan and medical surveillance above action levels.

3. Temporary Power and Job Site Electrical Safety — Temporary power panels require GFCI protection, grounding, and weather-rated enclosures per NEC Article 590. Lockout/tagout before servicing temp feeds; inspect cords for damage daily. NEC 1926 Subpart K applies on construction sites — only qualified electricians perform permanent connections.

Apply these to your specific scope, verify against project documents/local AHJ requirements, and confirm with your competent person or PE of record before field execution.
answers.cursor-agent: Under OSHA construction rules (29 CFR 1926.501), fall protection is generally required at 6 feet above a lower level for most walking-working surfaces. Use guardrails, safety nets, or personal fall arrest (or other allowed systems) as specified for the task. Exceptions and different trigger heights exist for some activities (e.g., scaffolds, steel erection have their own Subpart rules) â€” check the applicable Subpart, not only 501. Competent person must identify hazards; inspect harnesses, lanyards, and anchorage (typically 5,000 lb per worker for PFAS) before use. Do not treat 'we're only up a minute' as an exception.

cases.query: What is the critical path in a CPM schedule?

answers.auricrux-fca:
Auricrux construction corpus response (grounded, no live model reachable):

1. Critical Path Method Scheduling — CPM scheduling identifies the longest sequence of dependent activities (the critical path) with zero float; activities off the critical path have float that can absorb minor delays without moving substantial completion.

2. Change Order Pricing and Documentation — Price change orders with labor, material, equipment, sub markup, and overhead/profit consistent with the contract's markup schedule; document time impact with a fragnet showing the change tied into the critical path schedule.

3. Schedule Delay and Time Impact Analysis — A time impact analysis inserts a delay fragnet into the as-planned schedule to isolate its net effect on the critical path, distinguishing excusable/compensable delays (owner-caused) from non-excusable delays (contractor-caused).

Apply these to your specific scope, verify against project documents/local AHJ requirements, and confirm with your competent person or PE of record before field execution.
answers.cursor-agent: In CPM, the critical path is the longest path of dependent activities through the network â€” the chain with zero (or least) total float that sets the project finish date. Delay any critical activity and the finish slips one-for-one (absent acceleration). Near-critical paths with small float matter too. Build logic with real finish-to-start (and legitimate leads/lags), resource-load if needed, and update with actuals. A time impact analysis inserts a delay fragnet onto the then-current schedule to measure critical-path impact for COs/claims.

Three or more exits are required at higher thresholds (e.g., 501+ and 1,001+ in common IBC tables). Exit separation, travel distance, and common-path limits also apply. Always use the adopted code edition and occupancy classification for the project â€” do not memorize one number for all buildings.
